author: original (NevaIB)
title: The metallic model
bigPicture: Metals are a lattice of positive ions held together by a sea of delocalised electrons. Because those electrons can move and the bonding has no fixed direction, metals conduct, can be hammered into shape and are strong; the more charge and the smaller the ion, the stronger the bond.

keyIdeas.cue: How does the metallic bond explain metal properties?
keyIdeas.answer: Electrostatic attraction between a lattice of cations and delocalised electrons. Electrical conductivity: delocalised electrons move when a voltage is applied. Thermal conductivity: mobile electrons and vibrating ions pass energy along. Malleable and ductile: layers of ions can slide without breaking the bonding, as the electrons still hold them. Link uses to properties (Cu for wiring, Al for pans).

keyIdeas.cue: What affects the strength of a metallic bond?
keyIdeas.answer: Higher cation charge (more delocalised electrons) and smaller ionic radius → stronger bond → higher melting point. Across period 3: Na < Mg < Al. Down group 1: melting point falls as ions get larger.

keyIdeas.cue: Why do transition elements have high melting points and good conductivity (AHL)?
keyIdeas.answer: Both 3d and 4s electrons can delocalise, giving more delocalised electrons per atom and smaller, more highly charged ions, so stronger metallic bonding. Their chemical properties are in R3.4/S3.1.

keyTerms.def: Attraction between a lattice of cations and delocalised electrons.
Electrons not tied to one atom; free to move through the structure.
Can be hammered into shape without breaking.

workedExamples.title: Comparing melting points
workedExamples.prompt: Explain why magnesium (650 °C) melts at a higher temperature than sodium (98 °C).
steps: Mg²⁺ has a higher charge than Na⁺ and is smaller.
Mg contributes two delocalised electrons per atom; Na one.
Stronger attraction between cations and delocalised electrons.

misconceptions.right: In solid metals the delocalised electrons carry the current; ions are fixed.
Layers slide but the delocalised electrons keep bonding them: the bond is non-directional.

checkpoints: Layers of cations can slide over each other
Delocalised electrons still hold them; bonding non-directional

practice.prompt: Explain the trend in melting point from Na to Al.
checkpoints: Ion charge increases and radius decreases

practice.prompt: Explain why iron has a much higher melting point than calcium.
checkpoints: Fe can delocalise 3d as well as 4s electrons
More delocalised electrons and smaller ion → stronger metallic bond

paper1B.data: Melting points (°C): Li 180, Na 98, K 63, Rb 39.
paper1B.answer: Decreases down group 1: ionic radius increases, so the attraction between the 1+ ions and the delocalised electrons weakens.
